quiz.stem:
A 26-year-old man is brought to a Sydney emergency department after a motorbike crash. He is agitated and breathless. RR 36/min, HR 138 bpm, BP 76/40 mmHg, SpO2 82% on high-flow oxygen. Breath sounds are absent on the right, which is hyper-resonant. His neck veins are distended and the trachea is deviated to the left.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Rapid IV fluid bolus and reassess
Immediate decompression of the right pleural space
Intubate and ventilate before any other procedure
quiz.explanation:
This is **tension pneumothorax**: respiratory distress, hypotension, absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance on one side, distended neck veins and tracheal deviation away from the affected side. It is a **clinical diagnosis** and must be treated **immediately**, without waiting for imaging.

Decompress the right pleural space (needle decompression, or finger thoracostomy in trauma), followed by an intercostal catheter. Positive pressure ventilation before decompression can make a tension pneumothorax worse and precipitate arrest.

**Principle:** if you are thinking of ordering an X-ray for a suspected tension pneumothorax, you have already waited too long.
whyWrong: Waiting for imaging delays life-saving decompression.
CT is inappropriate in an unstable patient with a clinical diagnosis.
Fluid will not relieve obstructive shock from tension.
Positive pressure ventilation before decompression can worsen tension and cause arrest.

quiz.stem:
A 21-year-old man who smokes presents to an emergency department in Adelaide with sudden left-sided chest pain that started at rest 6 hours ago. He is mildly breathless only on climbing stairs. RR 16/min, HR 84 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air. Chest X-ray shows a small left apical pneumothorax. He has no lung disease.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observation with clear follow-up and safety-netting advice
Insertion of a large-bore intercostal catheter
Needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space
Admission for high-flow oxygen for 5 days
quiz.explanation:
This is a **small primary spontaneous pneumothorax** in a young smoker with **minimal symptoms** and normal observations. **Conservative management** (observation, analgesia, a repeat X-ray and follow-up) is appropriate, with advice to return immediately if breathlessness worsens.

He should be counselled to **stop smoking** (including cannabis), **avoid flying** until resolution is confirmed, and **avoid scuba diving** permanently unless he has definitive surgery. Surgery is for recurrence or persistent air leak.

Needle decompression is for tension. Large-bore drains are unnecessary here.
whyWrong: A large-bore drain is unnecessary for a small, minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax.
Surgery is for recurrence or persistent air leak, not a first small episode.
Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax.
Prolonged admission for oxygen is not required.

quiz.stem:
A 68-year-old man is admitted to a Brisbane hospital with pneumonia. After 4 days of IV antibiotics he still has fevers. Chest X-ray shows a moderate right pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yields turbid fluid: pH 7.05, glucose 1.8 mmol/L, LDH 1400 U/L, and Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change to oral antibiotics and discharge
Insert an intercostal catheter for drainage and continue antibiotics
quiz.explanation:
This is a **complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema**: persistent fever despite antibiotics, turbid fluid, **pH below 7.2**, low glucose, high LDH and organisms on Gram stain. Antibiotics alone cannot sterilise an infected pleural collection.

Management is **intercostal catheter drainage** plus continued, targeted antibiotics (including anaerobic cover per eTG). If drainage is poor or the effusion is loculated, intrapleural tPA with DNase or thoracic surgery (VATS decortication) is considered.

Talc pleurodesis is used for recurrent malignant effusions, not infection.
whyWrong: He is still febrile with an infected collection; discharge is unsafe.
Delaying drainage allows loculation and fibrosis.
This is an exudative infected effusion, not fluid overload.
Pleurodesis is for recurrent malignant effusions, not empyema.

lessons.title: Interstitial and occupational lung disease, and lung cancer
objectives: Recognise the features of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and sarcoidosis
Describe the lung diseases caused by asbestos, silica and coal dust, including the Australian engineered stone story
Identify the presentations and paraneoplastic syndromes of lung cancer
Know the investigation pathway and the National Lung Cancer Screening Program

sections.heading: Why this matters in Australia
sections.body:
**Lung cancer** is the leading cause of cancer death in Australia. Most cases are linked to smoking, but a significant minority occur in never-smokers. The **National Lung Cancer Screening Program** began on 1 July 2025.

**Occupational lung disease** is specifically examinable. Australia has one of the highest rates of **mesothelioma** in the world because of heavy asbestos use until it was banned nationally in 2003. **Silicosis** has resurged in stonemasons cutting **engineered stone** benchtops, leading Australia to ban the use of engineered stone from 1 July 2024. **Coal workers' pneumoconiosis** ("black lung") re-emerged in Queensland coal miners from 2015.

**Interstitial lung disease (ILD)** is a group of disorders causing inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most important.

sections.heading: Mechanisms
sections.body:
**Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)**: repeated epithelial injury with abnormal wound healing and progressive fibrosis, starting at the bases and periphery. Median survival without treatment is only a few years.

**Other ILD causes**: connective tissue disease (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis), drugs (**amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin**), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (bird fancier's, farmer's lung; mostly upper zone), sarcoidosis, radiation.

**Sarcoidosis**: non-caseating granulomas in multiple organs, typically young adults. Hypercalcaemia arises from granulomas converting vitamin D to its active form.

**Asbestos** fibres are long and thin, not cleared, and cause:

- **Pleural plaques**: benign, calcified, a marker of exposure
- Diffuse pleural thickening and benign effusions
- **Asbestosis**: lower lobe interstitial fibrosis
- **Mesothelioma**: malignant tumour of the pleura (or peritoneum) with a **latency of 20 to 40 or more years**, even after brief exposure; poor prognosis
- **Lung cancer**: risk multiplied with smoking

**Silica** (quarrying, sandblasting, stonemasonry, engineered stone) causes silicosis: upper lobe nodular fibrosis, **eggshell calcification** of hilar nodes, progressive massive fibrosis and increased risk of **TB**, lung cancer and autoimmune disease. Engineered stone has very high silica content, causing accelerated silicosis within years.

**Coal dust** causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis, with upper zone nodules and progressive massive fibrosis.

**Lung cancer types**:

- **Non-small cell** (most): adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, including in never-smokers; may have targetable EGFR or ALK mutations), squamous cell (central, smokers, cavitation, PTHrP hypercalcaemia)
- **Small cell** (central, smokers, rapid growth, early spread, SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert-Eaton)

sections.heading: How they present
sections.body:
**IPF**: older (usually over 60), progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough, **fine bibasal inspiratory ("velcro") crackles**, **clubbing**.

**Sarcoidosis**: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy found incidentally, cough, erythema nodosum, arthralgia, uveitis. **Löfgren syndrome** (erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthritis, fever) has a good prognosis.

**Occupational disease**: always take an **occupational history** (jobs, dates, protection). Plumbers, builders, electricians, carpenters, shipyard and power station workers, and home renovators (and their families from dust on clothes) had asbestos exposure. Mesothelioma presents with breathlessness from effusion, **dull chest wall pain** and weight loss.

**Lung cancer**: persistent cough (or change in a chronic cough), **haemoptysis**, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, recurrent or non-resolving pneumonia, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), finger clubbing.

| Syndrome | Features | Association |
|---|---|---|
| Pancoast tumour | Shoulder and arm pain, C8-T1 weakness, **Horner syndrome** | Apical tumour |
| SVC obstruction | Facial swelling, distended neck and chest veins, headache | Small cell, lymphoma |
| **SIADH** | Hyponatraemia with concentrated urine | Small cell |
| **Hypercalcaemia (PTHrP)** | Polyuria, confusion, constipation | Squamous cell |
| Ectopic ACTH | Hypokalaemia, hypertension, rapid Cushingoid features | Small cell |
| Lambert-Eaton | Proximal weakness improving with repeated use | Small cell |
| Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy | Painful wrists and ankles, clubbing | Non-small cell |

sections.heading: Work-up
sections.body:
**ILD**:

- Spirometry: **restrictive** pattern (reduced FVC, normal or high FEV1/FVC) with **reduced DLCO** (gas transfer)
- **High-resolution CT (HRCT)**: IPF shows a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: basal, subpleural reticulation and **honeycombing** with traction bronchiectasis
- Autoimmune serology to find connective tissue disease; multidisciplinary discussion confirms the diagnosis
- Sarcoidosis: chest X-ray or CT (hilar nodes), serum calcium, ACE (supportive only), tissue biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas (often via EBUS)

**Occupational**: chest X-ray and HRCT; confirm exposure history. Silicosis, mesothelioma and some pneumoconioses are notifiable in several jurisdictions (varies by state).

**Lung cancer**:

- **Chest X-ray** as the first test for persistent symptoms (cough over 3 weeks, haemoptysis), but a normal X-ray does not exclude cancer; proceed to **CT chest** if suspicion remains (Cancer Council Australia optimal care pathway)
- Any **haemoptysis in a person over 40 who smokes**, or unexplained persistent symptoms, needs urgent CT and referral to a lung cancer multidisciplinary team
- Tissue diagnosis: bronchoscopy, EBUS-guided sampling, or CT-guided biopsy; molecular testing for targetable mutations in non-small cell cancer
- Staging: PET-CT, brain MRI in selected patients
- Bloods: sodium, calcium, liver function

**National Lung Cancer Screening Program** (from July 2025): **low-dose CT every 2 years** for asymptomatic people aged **50 to 70** with at least a **30 pack-year** smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 10 years. Check the program site for current details; symptomatic people need diagnostic tests, not screening.

sections.heading: Crackles, clubbing and hilar nodes
sections.body:
| Finding | Consider |
|---|---|
| Fine bibasal crackles and clubbing | IPF, asbestosis, connective tissue ILD |
| Upper lobe fibrosis | Silicosis, coal, TB, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, ankylosing spondylitis |
| Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy | Sarcoidosis, lymphoma, TB, silicosis |
| Clubbing in a smoker | Lung cancer (COPD itself does not cause clubbing) |
| Coarse crackles, lots of sputum | Bronchiectasis |

sections.heading: Treatment and referral
sections.body:
**IPF**: refer to a respiratory ILD service. **Antifibrotics (nintedanib or pirfenidone)** slow decline in lung function and are PBS-listed under criteria. Supportive care: pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen for hypoxaemia, vaccination, smoking cessation, treat reflux, lung transplant assessment in selected younger patients, and early palliative care. Steroids are not recommended in IPF.

**Drug-induced ILD**: stop the drug; steroids in some.

**Sarcoidosis**: many resolve spontaneously and are monitored; oral corticosteroids for significant organ involvement (eyes, heart, nervous system, progressive lung disease, hypercalcaemia).

**Occupational disease**:

- Remove from exposure; smoking cessation.
- Screen silicosis patients for TB (latent and active).
- Workers' compensation and, for asbestos-related disease, specific compensation schemes; legal and financial advice is part of care.
- Mesothelioma: multidisciplinary oncology, pleural fluid management (indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis), palliative care.

**Lung cancer**:

- Managed in a **multidisciplinary team**. Early-stage non-small cell: surgery (lobectomy) or stereotactic radiotherapy. Locally advanced: chemoradiotherapy and immunotherapy. Metastatic: targeted therapy if a driver mutation is present, immunotherapy, chemotherapy.
- Small cell: chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy and immunotherapy; usually metastatic at diagnosis.
- **Oncological emergencies**: SVC obstruction (stenting, radiotherapy, steroids), hypercalcaemia (IV saline, bisphosphonate), spinal cord compression (dexamethasone, urgent MRI, radiotherapy).
- Early palliative care improves quality of life.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks it
sections.body:
- 70-year-old retired builder with unilateral pleural effusion and chest wall pain: **mesothelioma**; pleural plaques alone are benign.
- Young stonemason with breathlessness and upper zone nodules: **accelerated silicosis** from engineered stone; test for TB.
- Clubbing, velcro crackles, restrictive spirometry, low DLCO, basal honeycombing: **IPF**; antifibrotics, not steroids.
- Smoker with hyponatraemia and a central mass: **small cell** cancer with SIADH. Hypercalcaemia: **squamous**.
- Ptosis, miosis and arm pain in a smoker: **Pancoast**.
- Screening eligibility questions: age 50 to 70, 30 pack-years, current smoker or quit within 10 years, no symptoms.

keyPoints: IPF: older patient, velcro crackles, clubbing, restrictive spirometry with low DLCO, UIP on HRCT; antifibrotics.
Asbestos causes pleural plaques (benign), asbestosis, mesothelioma (20-40+ year latency) and lung cancer.
Silicosis: upper lobe nodules, eggshell hilar calcification, TB risk; engineered stone banned in Australia from July 2024.
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis re-emerged in Queensland from 2015.
Small cell: SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert-Eaton; squamous: PTHrP hypercalcaemia.
Persistent cough or haemoptysis in a smoker: chest X-ray then CT even if X-ray is normal.
National Lung Cancer Screening Program: low-dose CT every 2 years, age 50-70, 30 pack-years, smoking now or quit within 10 years.
redFlags: Haemoptysis in a smoker over 40
Persistent cough, weight loss or new clubbing in a smoker
Facial swelling and distended chest veins (SVC obstruction)
Horner syndrome with arm pain (Pancoast tumour)
Back pain with leg weakness in known cancer (spinal cord compression)

contrast.india: Silicosis in stone quarry and mining workers and byssinosis in textile workers are emphasised.
contrast.australia: Mesothelioma from past asbestos use and silicosis from engineered stone (now banned) are the headline issues.

contrast.india: No organised lung cancer screening program.
contrast.australia: National Lung Cancer Screening Program with low-dose CT for eligible high-risk people since July 2025.

quiz.stem:
A 72-year-old retired plumber presents to his GP in Wollongong with 2 months of increasing breathlessness and a dull ache in the right side of his chest. He lost 6 kg. He smoked until age 50. Examination shows stony dullness at the right base. Chest X-ray shows a large right pleural effusion with nodular pleural thickening.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.explanation:
A retired **plumber** (a classic asbestos-exposed trade) with a **unilateral effusion**, **dull chest wall pain**, weight loss and **nodular pleural thickening** has **mesothelioma** until proven otherwise. Latency after asbestos exposure is typically 20 to 40 or more years, which fits.

Work-up: pleural fluid cytology (often non-diagnostic), CT chest, and pleural biopsy (image-guided or thoracoscopic). He should be referred to a multidisciplinary team, and advised about asbestos-related disease compensation.

Pleural plaques are benign and do not cause effusions or pain. Asbestosis is interstitial fibrosis, not a pleural effusion. Heart failure effusions are usually bilateral.
whyWrong: HF effusions are usually bilateral, without chest wall pain or pleural nodularity.
Asbestosis is lower lobe interstitial fibrosis, not a unilateral effusion.
Plaques are benign and asymptomatic.
There is no fever or infective picture.
quiz.ausPearl: Australia has among the world's highest mesothelioma rates. The Australian Mesothelioma Registry collects cases, and asbestos-related disease compensation schemes exist in each state.

quiz.stem:
A 36-year-old stonemason who has cut kitchen benchtops for 12 years presents to his GP in Melbourne with 6 months of progressive breathlessness and dry cough. He has never smoked. Chest X-ray shows multiple small nodules in both upper zones and enlarged hila with peripheral calcification of the hilar nodes.

In addition to confirming the diagnosis and removing him from exposure, which of the following is most important to test for?
quiz.explanation:
This is **accelerated silicosis** from **engineered stone** (very high crystalline silica content): young stonemason, progressive symptoms after about a decade, **upper zone nodules** and **eggshell calcification** of hilar nodes. Australia banned the use of engineered stone from 1 July 2024 because of an epidemic of silicosis among young workers.

Silica impairs macrophage function and markedly increases the risk of **tuberculosis** (silicotuberculosis), so screening for latent and active TB is essential. He also has increased risk of lung cancer, autoimmune disease and CKD. Removal from exposure, notification where required (varies by state), workers' compensation and specialist referral are needed.

Serum ACE is non-specific and supports sarcoidosis, which does not explain his occupation-linked picture.
whyWrong: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes basal emphysema, not nodular upper lobe fibrosis.
CF presents much earlier with bronchiectasis and pancreatic insufficiency.
Aspergillus is not the key risk associated with silicosis.
Serum ACE is non-specific and does not change his management here.

quiz.stem:
A 66-year-old woman who smoked 40 pack-years presents to a GP in Hobart with 5 weeks of cough and a new hoarse voice. She has lost 4 kg. Blood tests show sodium 124 mmol/L with high urine osmolality, and normal thyroid and adrenal function. Chest X-ray shows a large left hilar mass.

Which type of lung cancer is most likely?
quiz.explanation:
A heavy smoker with a **central hilar mass** and **hyponatraemia with concentrated urine** (SIADH, after excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency) most likely has **small cell lung cancer**, which secretes ADH ectopically. Hoarseness suggests left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement by the hilar mass.

Small cell cancer is also associated with ectopic ACTH and Lambert-Eaton syndrome. Squamous cell cancer is also central but classically causes hypercalcaemia via PTHrP. Adenocarcinoma is usually peripheral.

She needs urgent CT and referral to a lung cancer multidisciplinary team, and careful sodium correction.
whyWrong: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral and not classically linked with SIADH.
Squamous cell cancer is classically associated with PTHrP hypercalcaemia.
Carcinoid tumours cause flushing and wheeze rather than SIADH in a heavy smoker.
Mesothelioma is pleural, not a hilar mass with SIADH.
